items.stem: A management board in Dhaka has worked together for ten years. At a meeting about a risky expansion, the chief executive announces her support first, and nobody raises concerns. One manager later says he had doubts but “didn’t want to spoil the mood”. (a) Identify two symptoms of groupthink in this situation. (b) Suggest two changes to the board’s decision-making.
items.answer: (a) Self-censorship (the manager kept doubts to himself) and illusion of unanimity (no one raised concerns). (b) The chief executive should speak last; appoint a devil’s advocate or bring in an outside expert.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of Janis’s theory of groupthink. Include at least one point about method.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): It identifies symptoms and preventive measures, such as a devil’s advocate, that organisations can use. Strength (real-world evidence): It is supported by analyses of real policy failures such as the Bay of Pigs invasion. Weakness (method): Evidence comes largely from retrospective case studies, which are open to interpretation and hindsight bias. Weakness (cohesion): Laboratory studies show cohesion does not always lead to groupthink, so the model may be oversimplified. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Describe three symptoms of groupthink.
items.answer: Illusion of invulnerability (overconfidence); direct pressure on dissenters to conform; self-censorship of doubts; illusion of unanimity; collective rationalisation of warnings; mindguards; stereotyped views of outsiders; belief in the group’s morality.

items.stem: ‘Groups make better decisions than individuals.’ To what extent do you agree?
items.answer: Arguments for: Groups combine knowledge and skills; teams with a balance of Belbin roles perform better. Discussion can expose errors that one person would miss. Arguments against: Groupthink (Janis) can lead cohesive groups to poor decisions, for example the Bay of Pigs invasion. Group polarisation can make decisions more extreme. Groups take longer and some members may contribute little (social loafing). Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: Evaluate Belbin’s team-role theory, including a discussion of reliability.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): It gives managers a practical tool to build balanced teams and understand conflicts between roles. Strength (research base): It was developed from years of observing real management teams in business games. Weakness (reliability): The self-perception inventory is self-report and has been criticised for weak reliability and validity. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Evaluate the Thomas–Kilmann model of conflict management, including a discussion of self-report.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): It helps managers and staff understand their own preferred styles and choose a more suitable one. Strength (flexibility): It recognises that every mode can be useful in some situations rather than prescribing one approach. Weakness (self-report): The TKI relies on self-report, so people may give socially desirable answers. Weakness (reductionism): Reducing conflict behaviour to two dimensions ignores emotions, power and culture. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of the Thomas–Kilmann model of conflict management. Include at least one point about flexibility.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): It helps managers and staff understand their own preferred styles and choose a more suitable one. Strength (flexibility): It recognises that every mode can be useful in some situations rather than prescribing one approach. Weakness (reductionism): Reducing conflict behaviour to two dimensions ignores emotions, power and culture. Weakness (self-report): The TKI relies on self-report, so people may give socially desirable answers. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “Tuckman’s stage in which the group agrees rules and roles and becomes cohesive”.
items.answer: Norming

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Describe three symptoms of groupthink. (b) Explain two ways an organisation could prevent groupthink.
items.answer: (a) Illusion of invulnerability (overconfidence); direct pressure on dissenters to conform; self-censorship of doubts; illusion of unanimity; collective rationalisation of warnings; mindguards; stereotyped views of outsiders; belief in the group’s morality. (b) Appoint a devil’s advocate to challenge ideas; the leader should not state a preference at the start; invite outside experts; split into sub-groups; hold a “second-chance” meeting.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per symptom described [3] (b) 1 mark each method, 1 mark each explanation [4]

items.stem: Explain one strength and one weakness of Janis’s theory of groupthink. One of your points must be about usefulness.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): It identifies symptoms and preventive measures, such as a devil’s advocate, that organisations can use. Weakness (cohesion): Laboratory studies show cohesion does not always lead to groupthink, so the model may be oversimplified.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each point: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation in the context of the study [4]

items.stem: A new project team in Mumbai has just been formed. In the first weeks members argued about who should lead and how work should be divided. Explain one limitation of Tuckman’s model.
items.answer: Not all groups pass through the stages in order; some skip or return to stages, and it was based on reviews of small groups rather than work teams.
items.markingKey: 1 mark limitation; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: Elena wants to find out whether teams with a balance of Belbin roles perform better than unbalanced teams. Design a field experiment to investigate this. Your plan must include: the sampling technique, ethical issues and how the dependent variable will be measured.
items.answer: Method: a field experiment. Manipulate the IV in a natural everyday setting; participants may not know they are being studied; standardise as much of the procedure as possible. Variables: IV: balanced or unbalanced team; DV: score in a business game. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Manila, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: ‘Conflict at work is always harmful.’ Evaluate this statement, using evidence from psychology.
items.answer: Arguments for: Conflict can cause stress, absence and poor communication. Unresolved conflict can lead to staff leaving. Arguments against: Moderate conflict can bring out new ideas and prevent groupthink. Thomas and Kilmann show that conflict can be handled constructively, for example by collaborating. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how Belbin’s theory could be used for team building. (b) In a revision session, a student says: “Belbin’s research was based on management teams playing business games.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Staff complete the self-perception inventory and observer ratings; managers identify missing or duplicated roles, then select or train members and discuss roles so that people understand each other’s contributions. (b) Correct. He observed teams at Henley Management College.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark measurement; 1 mark use in selection or discussion [2] (b) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain one strength of Belbin’s team-role theory in terms of research base.
items.answer: It was developed from years of observing real management teams in business games.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to research base; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: A design team in Auckland produces many creative ideas but often misses deadlines and makes careless errors. (a) Using Belbin’s theory, identify a role that the team probably lacks and explain why. (b) Identify a role the team probably has too many of. (c) Suggest how the manager could use Belbin’s ideas to improve the team.
items.answer: (a) Completer finisher (or implementer), who checks for errors and ensures deadlines are met. (b) Plant (creative ideas generator). (c) Assess members’ roles with the inventory, then recruit or reassign someone with completer-finisher strengths and discuss roles openly.

items.answer: Thomas–Kilmann conflict mode that is assertive and uncooperative: pursuing one’s own concerns at the other’s expense.

items.stem: Priya and Mei work in a hospital in Doha. Both want the same week of holiday, and only one can be absent. Priya insists, while Mei says nothing and lets Priya have the week, but is now resentful. Suggest how the manager could help them collaborate.
items.answer: Meet both, explore underlying needs (for example one needs travel dates, the other a family event) and find a solution such as splitting weeks or finding cover.

items.stem: ‘Groups make better decisions than individuals.’ Evaluate this statement, using evidence from psychology.
items.answer: Arguments for: Groups combine knowledge and skills; teams with a balance of Belbin roles perform better. Discussion can expose errors that one person would miss. Arguments against: Groupthink (Janis) can lead cohesive groups to poor decisions, for example the Bay of Pigs invasion. Group polarisation can make decisions more extreme. Groups take longer and some members may contribute little (social loafing). Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
